findings.title: The two lock guards that Trail of Bits finding 3 records as its fix are absent from the source, and the synced currency check that stands in their place skips address(0), which shares its balance with an ERC-20 address on five networks
findings.difference: On Ethereum no ERC-20 address reports the PoolManager's native balance. On five of the 21 networks one does: LegacyERC20ETH at 0xDeadDeAddeAddEAddeadDEaDDEAdDeaDDeAD0000 on Optimism and Zora, 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 on Polygon, the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 on Celo and 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 on Arc, where the figure is the native balance divided by 10^12. I read balanceOf(PoolManager) and eth_getBalance at one block per network and they agree on these five and on no candidate address of the other 16. Optimism, Polygon and Arc also have a fee controller whose collect function any account can call. Celo and Zora have no fee controller today.
findings.mechanism: 1. The report (printed page 33) describes the hazard: a fee collection between sync and settle lowers the balance, so the settle that follows credits less or reverts. Its fix review (printed page 62) records the fix as two guards: sync can be called only while the manager is unlocked, and collectProtocolFees reverts with ContractUnlocked while the manager is unlocked. 2. The source has neither guard. sync carries no modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). collectProtocolFees checks the caller and then reverts only when the currency is nonzero and equals the synced currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). _isUnlocked is declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60 and implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:392-394 and has no caller. The interface still says the function reverts if the contract is unlocked (src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40) and declares ProtocolFeeCurrencySynced and no ContractUnlocked error (line 17). The tests of the repository expect the source behaviour in both lock states (test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039) and call sync while locked (test/Sync.t.sol:36-41). 3. The check that replaced the guards closes the report's case when the collected id is the synced id. It compares ids and exempts address(0) with the comment that native settle uses msg.value. That reasoning assumes the native balance has no second id (A3). 4. Where a native face exists and a controller can be triggered, the report's sequence runs again across two ids: sync(face), collection of native fees, settle. My walk on the deployed PoolManagers of Optimism (block 159,929,377), Polygon (97,834,382) and Arc (32,774,161), with a stub placed at the controller address by state override, gave the same three answers on each: collection of the face id reverted with ProtocolFeeCurrencySynced, collection of address(0) succeeded inside the unlock while the face was synced and paid out the accrued native fees (0.0407 ETH, 714.3 POL and 53.28 USDC), and the settle that followed reverted with a Panic from the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360. On the other five controller networks the same walk with a stub token that returns the native balance of its argument gave the same answers. 5. A separate eth_call of collect((address,uint256)[]) with one entry for address(0) from an arbitrary account succeeded on all eight controllers, and each controller names one fixed TOKEN_JAR. 6. I traced who pays. Collection lowers protocolFeesAccrued by a checked subtraction before the transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56), writes no delta and no transient slot, and pays the recipient the controller names. The lower balance reduces the credit of the account that holds the face bracket in that same transaction, or reverts its settle. A payer that syncs, transfers and settles without calling other code in between cannot be interleaved. The caller of collect gains nothing. 7. Two further effects follow from the absent guards. Any code that runs earlier in a shared transaction can leave sync(X) and make a later collection of X revert (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-51), which contradicts the report's invariant UNI-ACTION-6 as worded (collectProtocolFees must not revert on valid input). The same stale sync makes a later native settle with value revert, which the ledger holds as F-071.
findings.impact: No loss of pool funds and no lasting freeze found. The account that syncs a native face and lets a native fee collection run before its settle loses credit equal to the collected amount or has its transaction reverted. Fee collection of a currency can be made to revert by an earlier sync in the same transaction. The finding extends F-014 from Ethereum to the eight networks with a controller and ties it to the audit record.
findings.preconditions: A fee controller that any account can trigger (Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Arc today). For the two id case also an address that reports the native balance (Optimism, Polygon and Arc today, and Celo and Zora once the owner sets a controller there). The affected party must itself hold a sync of the face while the collection runs.
findings.mitigations: Restore the lock check that the interface comment describes, or make the synced check cover address(0) as well. Contracts that harvest fees and settle in one transaction should collect before they sync. Routers should call sync themselves before each payment, native payments included.

findings.title: OpenZeppelin CR-01 records that noDelegateCall was added to all relevant external functions, and the source carries it on the four pool functions only
findings.difference: None found. The guard compares address(this) with an immutable (src/NoDelegateCall.sol:24-26). Earlier cycles tested on all 21 deployed PoolManagers that a DELEGATECALL into the unguarded functions uses the storage, transient storage and balance of the calling account, and on 20 networks that an EIP-7702 account that names the PoolManager behaves the same. The Avalanche endpoint did not resolve a delegation designator.
findings.mechanism: 1. The report (page 24) says the modifier on unlock was meant to stop proxies for licence reasons, that a custom unlock that writes the same lock slot got around it, and that the team added noDelegateCall to all relevant external functions. 2. In the source the modifier sits on initialize, modifyLiquidity, swap and donate (src/PoolManager.sol:117, 148, 190, 259). unlock, sync, take, settle, settleFor, clear, mint and burn carry none (lines 104, 279, 291, 300, 305, 310, 322, 332). The test double of the repository puts it on unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn (src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:58, 151, 156, 163, 176, 181), and test/NoDelegateCall.t.sol:63-82 expects the revert from modifyLiquidity, swap and donate only. 3. I checked whether the gap reaches funds. A delegatecall runs the settlement functions on the lock flag, deltas, claims and balance of the calling contract. No pool can be created or used that way, because all four pool functions revert with DelegateCallNotAllowed. The PoolManager itself contains no delegatecall (search of src outside src/test). The stated purpose of the fix, keeping pool logic from running behind a proxy, is met by the four guarded functions. 4. The cleared items of cycles 1, 3 and 6 reach the same result, the last one by a test on every network.
findings.impact: No effect on funds held by the PoolManager. A contract or delegated account that runs this code on itself exposes its own balances to flash use and to the booking of balance increases, which concerns only that account.
findings.preconditions: None for the gap itself. An effect needs an account that chooses to run PoolManager code in its own context.
findings.mitigations: Add the modifier to the six functions that the test double guards if the licence purpose is to cover the settlement layer as well. No change is needed for custody.

findings.title: Any account can set the starting price of a pool or move the price of an empty pool for free, and core takes no price or amount bound on the first deposit (OpenZeppelin M-03, acknowledged and not resolved)
findings.difference: None in the code path, which is the same on Ethereum. Networks differ in who can see a pending transaction, and I fetched no source on that for the 21 networks in this session. The variant that initializes a predictable PoolKey ahead of its creator needs no view of pending transactions.
findings.mechanism: 1. initialize accepts any caller and stores the caller's price (src/PoolManager.sol:117-134, src/libraries/Pool.sol:100-107). The price is not part of the pool id (src/types/PoolId.sol:11-15), and a second initialize reverts (Pool.sol:101). Whoever is first sets the price. 2. swap has no check for liquidity. With zero liquidity in range each step returns zero amounts and moves the price to the next tick or to the limit (Pool.sol:344-437, src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-106), so any account can move the price of a pool without in range liquidity to any value inside the bounds for a zero delta. 3. modifyLiquidity computes the two amounts from the stored price (Pool.sol:206-236) and accepts no minimum or maximum from the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184). 4. A provider that adds liquidity after the price was set away from the market deposits at that price, and the attacker then swaps against the position at the off market price. 5. Nothing in src closes this. The report records the team's answer that peripheral contracts add slippage protection. I did not read the periphery. 6. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers an eth_call of initialize from an arbitrary account for an unused PoolKey returned ticks 0, 138162, -887272 and 887271 for four prices of my choice.
findings.impact: The first liquidity provider of a pool who adds through code without amount bounds can lose part of the deposit, up to most of its value, to the account that set the price. Pools that already hold in range liquidity are not affected, because moving their price costs the swap amounts.
findings.preconditions: A pool that is not yet initialized or has no in range liquidity, and a provider that adds liquidity without checking the pool price or bounding the amounts. The attacker needs no role.
findings.mitigations: Initialize and add liquidity in one transaction with amount bounds, as the report's update says the periphery does. Integrations that call modifyLiquidity themselves should read slot0 and compare the price before they add.

findings.title: A pool id that resembles another pool's id can be mined through the hooks field of the PoolKey, and core gives a reader nothing to tell the two pools apart (Trail of Bits finding 6, unresolved)
findings.difference: None found. The report's method places a hook at a mined address with CREATE2. An account with a mined address and an EIP-7702 delegation serves the same purpose where delegation is live, which the ledger records as F-013.
findings.mechanism: 1. The pool id is the keccak256 hash of the five words of the PoolKey (src/types/PoolId.sol:11-15) and the hooks address is the fifth word (src/types/PoolKey.sol:11-22). 2. initialize constrains the hook address only through its low 14 bits and the dynamic fee rule (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127, src/PoolManager.sol:126), so 146 bits of the address are free to vary while currencies, fee and tick spacing equal those of a known pool. 3. Core stores every pool under its full 32 byte id (src/PoolManager.sol:93), so two pools never share state. The hazard is in displays that shorten the id: a mined id can match the first and last characters of the known pool's id. 4. The attacker's pool carries the attacker's hook, which has the powers listed in the hook permissions note of this repository. 5. The fix review marks the finding unresolved, and nothing in src addresses it.
findings.impact: A user who picks a pool by a shortened id, or an integration that matches pools by a prefix, can be led into a pool whose hook takes the swap input or blocks removal. Funds in the original pool are not touched.
findings.preconditions: The victim must choose the attacker's pool. The attacker must author the hook.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces should show and compare the full PoolKey with the hook address. Integrations should match pools by the full 32 byte id.

findings.title: The repository's note on hook permissions confirms that a hook can block liquidity removal for good and can take a caller's full amounts through return deltas, and core limits these effects to the hook's own pool and to the bits of its address
findings.difference: None found in core. The note assumes the hook is the contract its author deployed. Where the code behind a hook address can change (EIP-7702 delegation, Stylus expiry on the Arbitrum family), the ledger records that separately as F-013, F-003 and F-053.
findings.mechanism: 1. The note lists 27 effects. I read each against src and found that none is prevented and each is confined. 2. Blocking: every hook call that fails or returns a wrong selector reverts the action (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). A hook with a remove flag is called for every liquidityDelta at or below zero, a fee collection with delta zero included (Hooks.sol:201-205, 232-243), and core has no path that removes liquidity without that call (src/PoolManager.sol:156, 178). The note marks this case as funds that could be permanently locked. 3. Taking: a hook with a return delta flag gets its returned amounts booked to its own address, and the caller's delta is reduced by the same amounts (Hooks.sol:222-230, 234-242, 295-313, PoolManager.sol:181-183, 224-226). Core sets no upper bound on these amounts. The one bound is that a beforeSwap delta cannot turn an exact input swap into an exact output swap or the reverse (Hooks.sol:273-279), which is why a hook can take all of the specified amount of an exact input swap and none of the specified amount of an exact output swap, as the note says. 4. Confinement: return delta flags are honoured only together with their action flag (Hooks.sol:111-120), hook deltas are booked in the two currencies of the pool the hook is attached to (PoolManager.sol:381-384), the sum of caller delta and hook delta equals the pool delta in every branch, and a hook's own calls into the PoolManager skip its hooks (Hooks.sol:171-175, 217, 253, 293). 5. Front-running, back-running, sandwiching and just in time liquidity by a hook use ordinary swap and modifyLiquidity calls from inside the callback and need no special permission in core.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers and swappers of a pool with a hook depend on that hook for exit and for the amounts they receive. Pools without a hook and pools with another hook are not affected. This adds the repository's own statement of the hazard to F-004.
findings.preconditions: The victim uses a pool whose hook was written, or can be changed, by the attacker.
findings.mitigations: As the note says for each return delta case, routers should check the returned deltas against the caller's bounds. Providers should read a hook's remove path before they deposit. Nothing in core can be configured.

cleared.check: OpenZeppelin audit, C-01: an ERC-20 representation of the native currency lets one payment be credited twice, once as msg.value under address(0) and once as a balance increase under the token, which drains native pools (worked case Celo, with Polygon as a network where deltas can be inflated).
cleared.result: Closed in the source. Hazard in one sentence: sync the token face, pay with settle and value, then settle the face for the same inflow. Closing statements: a settle with value reverts while any token is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356); a native credit is taken from msg.value only when no currency is synced (353-354); every write of a nonzero synced currency also writes the reserves (285-286, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32), so a face synced after a native payment starts from the higher balance; a token settle clears the slot (361); the contract has no receive or fallback function and only settle and settleFor are payable (300-307). The report says the fix makes the next settle after a sync settle that currency or revert. The source is looser in one way: sync(address(0)) clears the slot without a settle (283, documented at src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:165-171). I walked the orders that this allows and each inflow is still credited under one id only, because the stale reserves are overwritten by the next token sync. Reliance: A1 (the synced currency lives in transient storage for one transaction and is rolled back on revert), A2 and A3 (native value reaches the PoolManager through settle, and anything forced in is credited once under one id). Per network: an address that reports the PoolManager's native balance exists on Celo (CELO token, transfer works), Arc (0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000, six decimals, transfer works), Polygon (0x1010, transfer of 1 without value returned false), Optimism and Zora (LegacyERC20ETH, transfer disabled). My query found no such answer from these candidates on the other 16 networks, and the ledger holds a face search for each of them. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers my walk with a stub token that returns the native balance of its argument gave: sync while locked succeeded, settle with 1000 wei reverted with NonzeroNativeValue, a zero value settle paid 0 and cleared the slot, settle with 1000 wei then credited 1000, a new sync and settle of the face paid 0, and a native take of 1000 closed the unlock. The real faces on Celo, Polygon, Arc, Optimism and Zora gave the same seven answers. The walk shows the contracts deployed today. The checkout was not compiled.

cleared.check: OpenZeppelin audit, security model and trust assumptions (page 9): core has no slippage protection, non-standard and malicious tokens are not supported, malicious hooks can take from users of their pool, and anyone can create a pool with any token.
cleared.result: These are stated limits and nothing in src closes them. What src provides is separation: pool state is stored per pool id (src/PoolManager.sol:93), deltas per caller and currency (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41), hook deltas are booked to the hook address in the two currencies of its pool (PoolManager.sol:181, 224, 381-384). Reliance: A2 and A4 for tokens, A7 for hooks. The ledger records where these fail per network (rebasing and reward tokens F-012, F-041, F-066, F-067, F-091, tokens that move or burn the PoolManager balance F-085, F-086, F-090, F-099, issuer controls F-057, F-080). cleared.check: OpenZeppelin audit, M-01: assembly blocks marked memory-safe wrote past the scratch space or over the free memory pointer (hook return data, the TickMisaligned error, two argument custom errors, the ERC-20 transfer call).
cleared.result: Closed. The hook return data is copied to memory at the free memory pointer, which is then advanced by the padded length (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:140-149). TickMisaligned and the two argument revert helpers build their data at the free memory pointer and revert at once (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:57-63, src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:49-79, 83-118). The single argument helpers write 36 bytes into the 64 byte scratch space (CustomRevert.sol:14-46). The ERC-20 transfer writes its 68 bytes of calldata at the free memory pointer, reads the answer into the first scratch word and zeroes the three words it used (src/types/Currency.sol:55-80). Reliance: A10 only, that MSTORE, MLOAD, RETURNDATACOPY and CALL behave as on Ethereum, which cycle 1 tested on every network.

cleared.check: OpenZeppelin audit, L-03: fromId turns a uint256 into a currency and drops the upper 12 bytes, so mint and burn could act on an id that differs from the currency. The report says the team added a mask to fromId.
cleared.result: Closed. fromId casts the id to uint160 (src/types/Currency.sol:114-118), which drops the upper 96 bits, and mint and burn pass currency.toId() to the claim ledger and not the raw argument (src/PoolManager.sol:324-327, 333-335). A raw id with upper bits therefore debits or credits the same currency and the same claim id as the clean one, and no claim can exist under an id with upper bits, because _mint is reached only from line 327. The direct ERC-6909 functions take raw ids (src/ERC6909.sol:25-56) and find a zero balance under any id with upper bits. The closing statement uses no property of the chain, so it holds on all 21 networks alike.

leads.question: OpenZeppelin M-03 is left to the periphery. Do the deployed PositionManagers (the 23,877 byte build on 19 networks and the 19,965 byte build on HyperEVM and Elysium) reject a mint or an increase when the pool price makes the amounts exceed the caller's maxima, and do the published SDK and the launch pad hooks with most pools pass maxima that bind?
leads.why: Core accepts any starting price from any account and moves the price of an empty pool for free (src/PoolManager.sol:117-134, src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437). If a widely used path adds first liquidity without a binding bound, an ordinary account can take part of that deposit on every network.

leads.question: Celo and Zora have an address that reports the PoolManager's native balance and no protocol fee controller. When the owner sets a controller there, is its collect function open to any account as on the eight networks that have one, and does a native fee collection then run while the face is synced?
leads.why: The synced currency check in collectProtocolFees skips address(0) (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49). On Optimism, Polygon and Arc that already lets a native collection lower the face balance between sync and settle. Celo is the one network where the face can also be paid out by take, so the walk should be repeated there once a controller exists.

leads.question: Which behaviour is the build for the 21 deployments meant to have: the lock check that src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 and the Trail of Bits fix review describe, or the synced currency check that src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52 and test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039 pin? If the lock check returns, which tests and which of the eight fee adapters change behaviour?
leads.why: The interface comment, the unused _isUnlocked hook and the audit record say one thing and the source and its tests say another. The ledger judged the present text harmless. A restored lock check would change what F-014 and F-071 describe and would make collection revert whenever it is triggered inside any unlock.

leadResults.answer: Answered for the OpenZeppelin report, the Trail of Bits report and the hook permissions note. The other three reports belong to unit core-code-audit-walk-b. I read the two reports and the note page by page and wrote one result for each of the 24 OpenZeppelin findings, the 6 Trail of Bits findings, the 7 code quality items of its appendix C, its invariant tables and static invariants, and the 27 effects of the note. No finding of these documents is open in a way that lets an ordinary account take or lock funds of others. The fix that a report describes is absent from the source in two places: the lock guards of Trail of Bits finding 3 (sync and collectProtocolFees), and noDelegateCall on unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn from OpenZeppelin CR-01. Both are findings of this file with severity info. For the first I confirmed on the deployed contracts of Optimism, Polygon and Arc that a native fee collection runs inside an unlock while the native face is synced and that only the holder of that sync pays. OpenZeppelin C-01 is closed by src/PoolManager.sol:356 and 285-286, and a walk on all 21 deployed PoolManagers, with the real face on Celo, Arc, Polygon, Optimism and Zora, gave no double credit. OpenZeppelin M-03 and Trail of Bits finding 6 are unresolved by decision of the team and are recorded as low findings. The hook effects are by design and are tied to F-004. Everything on chain was tested against the contracts deployed today, because the checkout cannot be built in this session.
